articles.title: MPA marks christening of first ammonia dual-fuelled vessel
articles.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore and Eastern Pacific Shipping have marked the christening of Terra Clove at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in Ulsan, South Korea. The 93,000 cubic metre Very Large Ammonia Carrier is EPS’s first ammonia dual-fuelled vessel and the first ammonia dual-fuelled commercial newbuild...
articles.body: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore and Eastern Pacific Shipping have marked the christening of Terra Clove at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in Ulsan, South Korea. The 93,000 cubic metre Very Large Ammonia Carrier is EPS’s first ammonia dual-fuelled vessel and the first ammonia dual-fuelled commercial newbuild vessel to be registered under the Singapore Registry of Ships. The vessel is equipped with Everllence’s first commercial ammonia dual-fuelled two-stroke marine engine, which successfully completed factory acceptance testing in April 2026. Delivery is expected in November 2026 following upcoming sea trials. Terra Clove is the result of a collaboration initiated in June 2022 by MPA, EPS, HHI and the American Bureau of Shipping to develop an ammonia dual-fuelled gas carrier under the Singapore flag. It is the first of two such vessels being built by HHI for EPS, both of which will be registered under the Singapore flag. Designed to transport ammonia as cargo and use it as propulsion fuel, the vessel incorporates specialised ammonia fuel handling, containment and safety systems. As Singapore’s flag administration, MPA worked closely with EPS, HHI, ABS and other industry partners on technical and regulatory compliance, reviewing the vessel’s design against IMO guidelines, participating in hazard identification and operability studies and providing regulatory guidance on ammonia detection, fuel system safety and emissions management. MPA also shared experience from earlier ammonia trials to support the development of onboard safety procedures and crew preparedness. Ang Wee Keong, Chief Executive of MPA, described Terra Clove as demonstrating that bringing together expertise from across the maritime value chain can address the uncertainties and investment risks inherent in new technology development, expressing hope that the vessel’s successful development will give the wider industry greater confidence in ammonia as a marine fuel. Cyril Ducau, CEO of EPS, described the naming as an important milestone toward making ammonia a viable marine fuel, emphasising that safe and practical operation remains the priority alongside technology development.

articles.title: DSV reports higher Q3 earnings as Schenker integration weighs on Road division
articles.summary: DSV reported higher revenue and operating profit in the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong earnings in its Air & Sea and Contract Logistics divisions. Revenue reached DKK 80.7 billion, compared with DKK 72 billion in the same period last year. Operating profit (EBIT) before special items increased to DKK 6.6...
articles.body: DSV reported higher revenue and operating profit in the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong earnings in its Air & Sea and Contract Logistics divisions. Revenue reached DKK 80.7 billion, compared with DKK 72 billion in the same period last year. Operating profit (EBIT) before special items increased to DKK 6.6 billion from DKK 5.4 billion. The quarterly result included DKK 300 million in gains from property disposals. Despite the earnings growth, DSV faced operational challenges in its European Road division following the integration of Schenker. Air & Sea and Contract Logistics support earnings DSV’s Air & Sea division reported EBIT before special items of DKK 4.28 billion, up 18.9% year-on-year. The improvement was mainly driven by cost savings from the Schenker integration. The division’s conversion ratio increased to 45.8%, compared with 38.6% a year earlier. Contract Logistics also delivered strong results, with operating profit rising 50.3% to DKK 1.67 billion. The division benefited from integration synergies, higher productivity and better warehouse capacity utilisation. Its results included DKK 105 million in property disposal gains. In contrast, Road division operating profit declined 35.1% to DKK 526 million, including DKK 195 million from property disposals. DSV attributed the decline to lower productivity and falling volumes following service disruptions linked to the Schenker integration. However, the company said Road operations had returned to normal by the end of September. DSV maintains Schenker synergy target DSV continues to expect annual synergies of approximately DKK 9 billion from the Schenker integration. However, some remaining savings in the Road division and certain Group functions are now expected to be realised in 2027. The company has also narrowed its full-year 2026 guidance for EBIT before special items to DKK 24–25 billion, compared with its previous range of DKK 23.5–25.5 billion. “We delivered earnings growth in a volatile market, driven by strong results in Air & Sea and Contract Logistics,” said Jens H. Lund, Group CEO of DSV. Meanwhile, DSV announced a new DKK 1.5 billion share buyback programme, its first since acquiring Schenker. The programme begins on October 21, 2026, and will run until February 1, 2027.

articles.title: New Crewsure Energy Program Provides Employee Benefits for Offshore Workers
articles.summary: Crewsure Insurance Services Limited (Crewsure) has announced the launch of Crewsure Energy, a new program that brings together traditional employee benefits with specialist Crisis Response protection, designed for companies employing personnel…
articles.body: New Crewsure Energy Program Provides Employee Benefits for Offshore Workers Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 © Crewsure Insurance Services Limited Crewsure Insurance Services Limited (Crewsure) has announced the launch of Crewsure Energy, a new program that brings together traditional employee benefits with specialist Crisis Response protection, designed for companies employing personnel working in the international energy and offshore sectors. The launch represents an expansion for Crewsure, as the company already provides specialist MLC crew benefits for personnel working aboard drilling ships and other maritime assets. Crewsure Energy now extends that expertise beyond the vessel to provide dedicated protection for employees and contractors working on offshore rigs and other declared energy operations. At its core are emergency medical expenses, personal accident and wages protection, with worldwide cover available subject to the policy terms and schedule. The medical section covers medical emergency treatment following illness or accident, while personal accident protection includes accidental death and permanent disability benefits and loss of wages cover and loss of baggage. The program also recognizes the operational consequences for an employer when a member of an overseas workforce can no longer continue their assignment. Cover can therefore include reasonable additional costs of recruiting and sending a replacement employee overseas following death, illness, bodily injury or qualifying compulsory quarantine. A distinguishing feature of Crewsure Energy is its integrated Crisis Response protection. Rather than treating employee benefits and security risks entirely separately, the program can respond to events including kidnap, detention, disappearance, hijack, hostage crisis, extortion, threats and virtual kidnap, with access to professional response consultants. Crisis benefits can extend considerably beyond the immediate incident, including response consultant costs, travel and accommodation, loss of salary, replacement key-person costs, legal and medical expenses, rehabilitation and job retraining, temporary security measures and other specified additional expenses. The program can also provide Emergency Political Repatriation and Relocation and Threat Repatriation, including specified travel and accommodation costs and, in qualifying circumstances, personal effects left behind and irrevocably lost following an emergency political repatriation. Emergency medical, inpatient and evacuation/repatriation assistance is supported by Northcott Global Solutions, with 24-hour assistance available, while the Crisis Response section provides access to specialist response consultants. The Medical Insurance, Personal Accident Insurance, Sick Pay and Crisis Response insurance is underwritten by certain underwriters at Lloyd's of London.

articles.title: Shipbuilding: Bayonne Drydock Gets MARAD Grant
articles.summary: Bayonne Drydock & Repair Corp. has secured a $673,123 grant from the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD) to upgrade surface preparation equipment and expand workforce training at its ship repair facility in the Port of New York and New Jersey.Awarded through MARAD's Small Shipyard Grant Program…
articles.body: Shipbuilding: Bayonne Drydock Gets MARAD Grant Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 Members of Bayonne Drydock’s Executive Leadership Team pose with Congressman Rob Menendez, NJ State Senator Angela McKnight, NJ Assemblyman Jerry Walker, Mayor Sharon Nadrowski, and Bayonne City Council Image courtesy BDD Bayonne Drydock & Repair Corp. has secured a $673,123 grant from the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD) to upgrade surface preparation equipment and expand workforce training at its ship repair facility in the Port of New York and New Jersey. Awarded through MARAD's Small Shipyard Grant Program , the funding will be combined with the shipyard's own investment to purchase automated ultra-high-pressure hydro-blasting and surface preparation equipment. The improvements are intended to increase productivity, reduce vessel turnaround times and enhance the yard's ability to service commercial and government vessels. The investment includes an integrated robotic hydro-blasting system, an additional surface preparation unit and supporting spare parts. Funding will also support training for the shipyard's workforce of more than 300 employees, enabling personnel to operate and maintain the new equipment. "This vital federal investment allows us to modernize our surface-preparation infrastructure with state-of-the-art robotic technology," said Ryan Patrick Woerner, Executive Vice President and General Counsel of Bayonne Drydock. Woerner said the additional equipment will improve operational productivity, limit downtime and provide employees with tools to support maritime readiness. The latest award continues a series of MARAD-supported capital improvements at the Bayonne facility. In 2018, the shipyard received $1.08 million for upgrades to its graving dock and welding equipment. Another $730,477 grant followed in 2023 for hydro-blasting equipment and telehandlers. Founded in 1997, Bayonne Drydock operates a full-service repair facility at the former Military Ocean Terminal in Bayonne, New Jersey. Its principal infrastructure includes a 1,092-foot graving dock and a 1,280-metric-ton mobile boat hauler. The yard provides scheduled maintenance, drydocking, heavy repairs and emergency services for commercial and government vessels. Bayonne Drydock’s Executive Vice President and General Counsel Ryan Patrick Woerner addresses dignitaries and the Bayonne Workforce at the Press Conference. Image courtesy BDD

articles.summary: SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII is expected to return to its Fort Schuyler campus by mid-November after the federal government abruptly changed plans for a months-long deployment...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy SUNY Maritime College SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII is expected to return to its Fort Schuyler campus by mid-November after the federal government abruptly changed plans for a months-long deployment supporting the U.S. Navy. The reversal comes just weeks after the vessel departed New York for Norfolk, Virginia, where it was scheduled to undergo maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of a classified national security mission. In an October 21 message to the college community, SUNY Maritime President Rear Admiral John A. Okon confirmed the change. “I am pleased to share an important update on Empire State VII. The federal activation plan has changed, and the ship is now expected to return to Fort Schuyler for academic use, ship work, and with watches resuming no later than the middle of November,” Okon wrote. The announcement marks a significant shift from the original plans outlined by the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD), which ordered the vessel’s activation in August for an anticipated 170-day federal mission. An August 28 decision memorandum reviewed by gCaptain said the ship was needed to meet an urgent Military Sealift Command requirement and that no other suitable vessel was available within the required timeframe. Maritime Administrator Stephen Carmel described the activation as a “compelling strategic necessity.” The ship subsequently departed New York for Norfolk on September 30, with plans to remain there through October 30 for maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of follow-on operations supporting the Navy. The nature and destination of those operations were never publicly disclosed. It remains unclear what prompted the change in plans, whether the original military requirement has been withdrawn or reassigned, or how much of the planned work in Norfolk has been completed. For SUNY Maritime, however, the early return is welcome news. The vessel’s absence had threatened to disrupt academic programs, shipboard training and the sea time cadets need to qualify for U.S. Coast Guard licenses. “Empire State is more than a training ship. It is a classroom, a laboratory, and an essential part of the Maritime experience,” Okon said. Okon previously warned that losing the ship for much of the academic year would create significant challenges, and he pressed MARAD to return the vessel by February to keep the college’s 2027 Summer Sea Term on schedule. The revised timeline would bring the ship home roughly three months earlier than that requested deadline. Empire State VII , delivered in 2023, is the first of five purpose-built National Security Multi-Mission Vessels (NSMVs) developed by MARAD. The ships are designed primarily to train future merchant marine officers while also providing the federal government with additional sealift and emergency response capabilities. The vessel’s activation was expected to provide an early test of the NSMV program’s dual-use concept, demonstrating how a federally owned training ship could be called into service for national security missions. Instead, the shortened deployment raises questions about the circumstances behind the original urgent military requirement and the subsequent decision to release the vessel. “We will continue working with MARAD to confirm the exact details of the ship’s return and ensure we are ready to resume normal operations,” Okon said. articles.title: Panama Canal transits rise 4.1% in FY2026 as tonnage reaches 521 million
articles.summary: The Panama Canal recorded higher vessel traffic and tonnage in fiscal year 2026, supported by stronger activity in energy shipping and the container shipping sector. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits between October 2025 and September 2026, an increase of 4.1% compared with 13,404 transits in the previous...
articles.body: The Panama Canal recorded higher vessel traffic and tonnage in fiscal year 2026, supported by stronger activity in energy shipping and the container shipping sector. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits between October 2025 and September 2026, an increase of 4.1% compared with 13,404 transits in the previous fiscal year. Total tonnage reached 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, up 6.5% from 489.2 million PC/UMS tons in FY2025. The Panama Canal Authority reported the results on October 21, highlighting continued demand for the waterway and improved operating conditions. Neopanamax traffic supports growth Larger vessels contributed to the canal’s performance during the year. Ships using the Neopanamax locks accounted for 52.2% of total PC/UMS tonnage. Tonnage through these locks increased by 8.2% compared with the previous fiscal year. The canal also maintained a maximum permitted draft of 50 feet throughout the dry season, supporting vessel operations despite ongoing water management challenges. Meanwhile, total revenue increased by 16.6% to approximately $6.6 billion. The Panama Canal Authority noted that these financial figures remain unaudited. The authority continues to advance its long-term development plans under Vision 2025–2035, including the Río Indio Lake Project. Last-minute transit reservations restored Alongside its annual results, the Panama Canal Authority announced the immediate reinstatement of its Last-Minute Reservation service for vessels using the Panamax locks. The service provides ships without an existing reservation with another opportunity to secure a transit slot when capacity becomes available. However, the allocation of these slots remains at the canal authority’s discretion. The decision follows improvements in water management and recent rainfall levels approaching historical averages in the canal’s watershed. The authority said it will continue monitoring water conditions and announce further operational adjustments when necessary. The latest results reflect increased canal activity, while the return of last-minute reservations provides additional flexibility for shipping companies planning transits through the waterway.

articles.body: Houthi Attacks Drive Oil Prices to Five-Month High Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 © Adobe Stock/vadish Oil prices climbed about 2% to a five-month high on Thursday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the key exporting region. Brent futures rose $2.42, or 2.2%, to $111.24 a barrel at 10:45 a.m. EDT (1445 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose $1.14, or 1.2%, to $98.29. That drove Brent into technically overbought territory for a third time in a week and set for its highest close since May 18. Saudi Aramco has told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen's Houthis intensifies. Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned group pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb, a shipping chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth. "Reports of Middle East crude oil exports exceeding pre-conflict levels are more than countered by attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and on its oil infrastructure," PVM Oil analyst Tamas Varga said. "No de-escalation is anticipated until the US midterm elections, which should keep oil prices elevated." Morgan Stanley analysts estimated that Middle East crude oil exports were around 17 million barrels per day last week. Crude exports from the region averaged about 18 million bpd in the 12 months before the start of the Iran war, according to Kpler. In the US, refiner Valero Energy posted its highest-ever quarterly profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict sent refining margins soaring during the third quarter. AROUND THE WORLD Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the two sides kept up a barrage despite the latest US push to end the war. Russia said on Wednesday it was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St Petersburg. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November. Russia was the world's third-biggest crude oil producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, US energy data showed. Sanctions designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine have helped support oil prices. Any deal to end the war which began with Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 could allow Russia to export more. Senior Russian political and energy officials urged the European Union on Thursday to reconsider its plans to ban imports of Russian LNG, arguing the bloc's low storage levels had put Europe in a precarious position. The European Parliament, meanwhile, approved a three-year delay to EU methane emissions rules for oil and gas imports, after pressure from governments including France and the US. In Libya, an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Thursday. (Reuters)

articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd expects more services to return to Suez Canal
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd expects additional shipping services to return to the Suez Canal as maritime conditions in the Red Sea gradually improve, according to the Suez Canal Authority (SCA). The development was discussed during a meeting between SCA Chairman Adm. Ossama Rabiee and Juan Pablo Richards, Hapag-Lloyd’s Regional Head...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd expects additional shipping services to return to the Suez Canal as maritime conditions in the Red Sea gradually improve, according to the Suez Canal Authority (SCA). The development was discussed during a meeting between SCA Chairman Adm. Ossama Rabiee and Juan Pablo Richards, Hapag-Lloyd’s Regional Head for Southern Europe, on October 21. According to the SCA, two Hapag-Lloyd services connecting Asia and Europe are already operating through the Suez Canal. Further services are expected to return in the coming period, although no specific routes or dates have been announced. Hapag-Lloyd monitors Red Sea security conditions During the meeting, Richards highlighted the shipping company’s continued cooperation with the Suez Canal Authority. He explained that Hapag-Lloyd is closely monitoring developments in the Red Sea, particularly maritime safety conditions. These assessments will guide decisions on possible adjustments to sailing schedules as vessel traffic gradually returns through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Suez Canal. The announcement did not identify the two services currently using the waterway or provide a timetable for additional services to resume transits. Meanwhile, Rabiee reaffirmed the canal’s readiness to accommodate returning shipping services. He also expressed hope that Hapag-Lloyd would eventually restore all its services through the waterway. The SCA chairman highlighted ongoing improvements to navigation services and the authority’s fleet, aimed at meeting the operational requirements of shipping companies. Further cooperation discussed Beyond vessel transits, the two sides explored opportunities to expand their cooperation. Richards expressed interest in potential collaboration between the SCA’s Maritime Training and Simulation Academy and the Damietta Alliance Container Handling Terminal, also known as Tahya Misr 1, at Damietta Port. The proposed cooperation would focus on training ship masters, reflecting Hapag-Lloyd’s involvement as a major investor in the Damietta Alliance Terminal. The discussions come as shipping companies continue evaluating the security and operational conditions required for a broader return to the Suez Canal route. While Hapag-Lloyd anticipates additional services returning, the company has not announced a confirmed schedule for further route changes.

articles.title: China Tightens Grip on Global Shipbuilding as Order Book Hits Near-Record High
articles.summary: China has further cemented its dominance of global shipbuilding, capturing nearly three-quarters of new orders over the past year as the industry’s order book approaches record levels, according to new...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The 24,188 TEU capacity OOCL Spain pictured at the Nantong COSCO KHI Ship Engineering (NACKS) shipyard in Nantong, China. Photo courtesy OOCL China has further cemented its dominance of global shipbuilding, capturing nearly three-quarters of new orders over the past year as the industry’s order book approaches record levels, according to new analysis from BIMCO. The global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2 million compensated gross tonnage (CGT) as of September 1, 2026, up 13% from 180 million CGT a year earlier. While slightly below the all-time high of 210.4 million CGT reached in May, the backlog remains above the previous record of 195.4 million CGT set in 2008. Chinese shipyards have been the biggest beneficiaries of the ordering boom, securing 74% of all CGT contracted over the past 12 months. China now controls 64% of the global order book, well ahead of South Korea at 19% and Japan at just 6%. China’s lead is even more pronounced across the major commercial shipping sectors. Its yards hold more than 72% of the order book in each of the six main vessel categories, including containerships, tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers, other dry cargo ships and RoRo vessels. Together, those segments account for 88% of the global order book. Containerships are driving much of the growth. “Container ships dominate both the order book and its growth over the past 12 months. They account for 30% of CGT on order and 68% of the increase during the past year,” said Niels Rasmussen, BIMCO’s Chief Shipping Analyst. Chinese yards hold an especially commanding 81% share of the global containership order book. But the massive backlog also presents a growing challenge for shipbuilders, particularly in China, where scheduled deliveries are set to far exceed recent production levels. Based on each country’s highest annual output between 2021 and 2025, Chinese shipyards have enough orders to keep them busy for an average of 4.2 years. That compares with just 1.9 years for South Korean yards and 1.7 years for Japanese yards. The challenge is the sheer volume of ships scheduled for delivery. Combined output from China, South Korea and Japan reached 40.1 million CGT in 2025, but scheduled deliveries climb to 55.9 million CGT in 2027 and 60 million CGT in 2028. China faces the steepest increase, with its shipyards scheduled to deliver a record 44 million CGT in 2028, nearly double the 22.7 million CGT delivered in 2025. Meeting those commitments will require a significant increase in production capacity. BIMCO estimates that if capacity is instead measured against the highest annual output delivered or scheduled between 2021 and 2030, China’s order book coverage falls to 2.1 years, compared with 1.6 years for both South Korea and Japan. The figures highlight a potential downside to China’s rapid shipbuilding expansion. articles.title: Putin’s War On Ukraine Puts Oil Giant Rosneft Under Mounting Pressure
articles.summary: Along Russia’s remote Arctic coast last month, Igor Sechin stood beside a waiting tanker in the freezing cold with a message for Vladimir Putin: After years of construction, the country’s next great oil frontier was finally coming to life.

(Source: Rosneft) (Bloomberg) — Along Russia’s remote Arctic coast last month, Igor Sechin stood beside a waiting tanker in the freezing cold with a message for Vladimir Putin: After years of construction, the country’s next great oil frontier was finally coming to life. Hundreds of miles of pipeline now connected oil fields to storage tanks and a new port for Vostok Oil, part of an almost $50 billion investment. With Putin watching by video link, Sechin, the powerful head of state-run Rosneft PJSC, asked to begin loading the first tanker with crude. “Permission granted,” Putin said. The ceremony carried particular weight for Russia’s increasingly battered oil industry. Years of war and sanctions are making it harder for oil producers — including Rosneft, the nation’s largest — to maintain volumes today while developing reserves for tomorrow. Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project was supposed to show Russia could still do both. Sechin said it would add as much as 10% to the country’s current output by 2030 and supply millions of barrels to world markets for a century or more. But the milestone obscured a more complicated reality: Years behind schedule, Vostok Oil is still far from becoming Russia’s new oil province. The vast majority of crude flowing through the costly new Arctic network has been diverted from fields that have been producing for years. Just before the terminal opened in September, new oilfields in the Payakha cluster, expected to become key assets of Vostok Oil, accounted for less than 5% of its flows, according to a person familiar with the data, who asked not to be identified to discuss sensitive matters that aren’t public. Satellite imagery shows development continuing, but bringing those fields up to scale will require years more work and investment, according to Bloomberg analysis of the imagery and conversations with analysts. “The development of the company’s fields is carried out in a planned manner, which allows maximum efficiency to be extracted both from existing fields and from new projects,” Rosneft said in a statement, adding that production ramp-ups at Vostok Oil depend on market needs and general economic conditions. Viktor Kurilov, a senior analyst on the oil markets team at Rystad Energy, said building out Vostok Oil “is just one of the challenges Rosneft — and the Russian oil industry — is facing.” Among them is Ukraine’s dramatically expanded campaign of drone strikes against the country’s oil sector, which is inching closer to Vostok Oil facilities and repeatedly damaging refineries run by Rosneft and others in the European part of Russia. One of its biggest, Ryazan, which supplies fuel to Moscow and surrounding regions, has been shut for more than half the time since it was first attacked in May and has run well below full capacity when operating, according to damage assessments seen by Bloomberg. In turn, Rosneft’s finances are suffering. The company’s profits are falling and debt is rising despite what should have been a windfall from the Iran war. Rosneft officials have expressed concern that even a few more months of the war in Ukraine could leave lasting damage across the business, according to people familiar with the matter. The mounting toll to Rosneft and Russia’s wider oil industry helps explain why stopping Ukraine’s strikes on refineries has become such a priority for Moscow. This month, Putin and US President Donald Trump struck a deal opening the door to American purchases of Russian diesel, providing a potential boost as Washington also pressed Kyiv to halt the attacks, an important contributor to the squeeze on global diesel supplies. But an attempted energy truce quickly unraveled, narrowing Rosneft’s avenues for relief — and raising the stakes for a government that gets roughly a fifth of federal revenues from oil and gas. This story is based on conversations with people familiar with the situation at Rosneft, expert analysis and a series of documents reviewed by Bloomberg over the last six months, including damage assessments and company plans for protecting and repairing refineries. Vostok Oil was conceived in a different era, when Russia’s oil refineries were not under constant threat of Ukrainian attacks and production was expected only to grow. Laying out his plans to Putin at a Kremlin meeting in February 2020, Sechin described a vast new Arctic oil province that would create jobs and industry in a remote part of the country. One goal, he said, was to turn the Northern Sea Route into a major global energy corridor. The project was also intended to address a longer-term challenge: Many of Russia’s biggest oilfields had been producing since Soviet times, making new reserves increasingly important to offset their decline. The ambition attracted foreign investors, including commodity trading giant Trafigura, which acquired a 10% stake in 2020, and a Vitol-led consortium, which bought another 5% the following year. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 upended those plans. Both Trafigura and the consortium exited, while Western sanctions restricted access to the technology and equipment needed to develop Vostok Oil and build specialized tankers capable of navigating icy waters. As the war dragged on, Ukraine intensified its campaign against Russia’s infrastructure, increasingly targeting the refineries that turn crude oil into fuel. So far this year, Ukrainian drones have carried out at least 114 strikes on Russian refineries, more than double the number over the same period last year, according to a Bloomberg tally, based on public statements from both countries. The attacks have pushed Russian refinery runs to multi-year lows, triggered fuel shortages and forced Moscow to restrict exports of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Rosneft has borne a significant share of the damage. The company operates 12 refineries accounting for about a third of Russia’s total oil-processing capacity. Of 15 confirmed drone strikes on the country’s oil-processing plants in September, five targeted major Rosneft facilities supplying fuel to European Russia, the largest consuming region, according to Bloomberg’s tally. Rosneft is “taking appropriate measures to ensure the security and operation of our plants,” and will continue to make sure they are protected, the company said in its statement. “Not a single company petrol station has been closed, and consumers receive fuel in full at stable prices,” it said. In March, while reflecting on Rosneft’s 2025 results, Sechin, a longtime Putin ally, said Russia’s oil producers had faced a “perfect storm” of low oil prices, Western sanctions and soaring borrowing costs. Since then, repeated attacks have forced some of Rosneft’s biggest refineries to operate at reduced capacity or shut altogether. Ryazan has been among the hardest hit, repeatedly coming under attack as Rosneft has sought to restore operations. Another refinery, Syzran, has spent much of the past six months either completely shut or operating at less than a third of capacity, according to data reviewed by Bloomberg, and the company’s Tuapse refinery on the Black Sea coast has been offline since April. Rosneft has managed to restart some refineries within weeks of an attack, only to see them struck again as repairs are completed or nearing completion. The need to repeatedly repair damaged equipment is straining operations and causing costs to pile up to levels that Rosneft officials have privately warned cannot be sustained long-term, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive information. Some plants have deliberately slowed repairs as a result, stretching work that should take days into weeks, the people said. Efforts to protect the facilities with shipping containers, nets and steel cables have proved ineffective against swarms of drones, according to company plans reviewed by Bloomberg. The damage is particularly difficult to repair when strikes hit complex secondary units such as catalytic crackers, reformers and hydrocrackers, whose parts would previously have been sourced from the West. Sanctions are compounding the problems by restricting access to replacement equipment, forcing Rosneft to rely on Russian-made copies and Chinese imports that can take months to obtain and are not always compatible with existing machinery, people familiar with the matter said. More broadly, the International Energy Agency said drone strikes on Russian refineries are having a “cumulative negative effect.” In September, the agency cut its outlook for Russian oil processing over the next 18 months to around 4 million barrels a day, roughly 30% below prewar levels. The financial toll is mounting. Rosneft’s first-half net income fell by almost a fifth to 200 billion rubles ($2.4 billion). Its ratio of net debt to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization rose to 1.8 times at the end of June, the highest in more than five years, according to quarterly statements dating back to 2020, though three reports over the period don’t disclose the ratio, making estimations of the exact size and scope more challenging. To be sure, conditions have improved since then. Middle East disruptions have pushed the price of Russia’s Urals crude used for tax calculations above $90 a barrel, more than double its level at the start of the year, while Moscow is providing billions of rubles in subsidies to domestic fuel producers, including Rosneft, in recent months. Russia’s central bank has also cut its key rate from a record 21% to 14% over the past two years, though Rosneft has complained that the pace of reductions is “clearly insufficient.” The company’s financial picture and the extent of damage to its infrastructure are being closely monitored by the Qatar Investment Authority, which owns 18.46% of Rosneft and has seen its dividend payments fall sharply during the Ukraine war, according to three Qatari officials familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive information. QIA hopes for a swift end to the conflict so its investment is protected longer-term, one of the people said. QIA declined to comment. Rosneft’s problems have coincided with signs of distress at Credit Bank of Moscow PJSC, which market participants and officials view as being in the orbit of Sechin and his oil giant. MKB, as it is known, is dealing with $8 billion in problem loans, Bloomberg reported last month. That development highlights how both Russia’s energy and banking sectors are coming under strain at the same time, a dynamic that Russian finance officials have expressed concern about, people familiar with the matter said. Rosneft said in its statement that its “relations with MKB, as with other Russian banks, are standard,” adding that “neither Rosneft nor its Chief Executive Officer are or have ever been beneficiaries of MKB.” Rosneft faces another financial challenge: the enormous spending still required at Vostok Oil. The project remains heavily dependent on production from Vankor, a group of established fields that began pumping crude in 2009. Its new Arctic terminal gives Rosneft another route to market for that oil, but does little on its own to increase Russia’s output. Rystad Energy, which has analyzed satellite imagery of construction at the project, expects Vostok Oil to produce about 310,000 barrels a day in 2027, with around 90% coming from the Vankor cluster, where fields have been producing for years. Output could rise to 440,000 barrels a day by 2030 — well short of the roughly 1 million Sechin has promised — with the new Payakha fields contributing only about 80,000 barrels a day, according to the consultancy. Getting the oil to market is another obstacle. Rosneft needs specialized tankers to navigate frigid Arctic waters, but Western sanctions have complicated efforts to build them. At least 30 would be needed by 2030 to transport Vostok Oil’s planned output, according to Sergey Vakulenko, an industry veteran and scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “They simply don’t exist today,” he said. With Russia’s war in Ukraine well into its fifth year, Putin has secured a potential reprieve from Washington. In an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump, the Russian president said Russia would partially relax its diesel export ban, releasing thousands of barrels a day into the global market. It’s unclear what, if anything, Russia will receive in return. But in the days since, Ukraine has faced temporary restrictions on its military access to SpaceX satellite technology and US intelligence. For Trump, the immediate concern was closer to home. Diesel prices had surged to near-record levels ahead of November’s congressional elections, squeezed by the war in Iran and disruptions to global fuel supplies. The agreement was intended to help bring prices down, though US officials have acknowledged it is unlikely to have much effect on the international diesel market. Washington also pressed Kyiv to halt refinery strikes that had constrained Russian exports. “Unless President Putin agrees to stop attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure, or President Trump agrees to give Ukraine additional offensive and defensive capabilities, Kyiv is unlikely to abide by a unilateral ceasefire,” said Fernando Ferreira, director of geopolitical risk at Rapidan Energy Group. The limits of the arrangement soon became apparent. Neither Russia nor Ukraine confirmed the energy ceasefire Trump subsequently announced, and Kyiv resumed refinery attacks last week after accusing Moscow of continuing strikes on its energy infrastructure. Even if the diplomacy eventually produces a more durable pause, Ukraine is already changing the battlefield. In 2022, its attacks reached targets some 650 kilometers (404 miles) from the border. By July this year, drones had struck the Omsk refinery deep in western Siberia, roughly 2,500 kilometers away. Vostok Oil’s Arctic terminal lies another 800 kilometers beyond that, still outside Ukraine’s demonstrated reach. But the vast distances that have long sheltered Russia’s most remote energy assets offer less reassurance than they once did: If the range of Ukrainian drone strikes continues expanding at its recent pace, Vostok Oil could plausibly come within reach within months. At last month’s opening ceremony, Sechin was still looking ahead. Bundled against the cold beside the Valentin Pikul , he told Putin that Vostok Oil would ship 30 million tons of crude as early as the second half of 2027. It was another sign of how much the project has suffered: The terminal was meant to be ready for that volume two years ago. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Photo courtesy McAllister Towing The global fleet of dual-fuel containerships and vehicle carriers has surpassed 500 vessels, with shipowners committing more than $200 billion to ships capable of running on alternative fuels, according to new figures from the World Shipping Council (WSC). The latest WSC Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard shows 503 dual-fuel vessels in service as of September 2026, a 41% increase from 358 a year earlier. Another 849 ships are on order, bringing the combined total to 1,352 vessels. The figures highlight the scale of investment underway as container lines and vehicle carriers prepare for a transition to lower-emission fuels, even as uncertainty over future environmental regulations continues to cloud the industry’s outlook. “The container ship and vehicle carrier industry have committed more than $200 billion to ships that can run on cleaner fuels, with more than 500 already sailing and hundreds more on the way,” said WSC President and CEO Joe Kramek. “The investment is happening, but these ships need commercially competitive alternative fuels to deliver their full potential to reduce emissions.” Dual-fuel vessels are designed to operate on conventional marine fuels as well as alternative fuels, giving operators flexibility as new fuel supplies and infrastructure develop. However, their ability to reduce emissions depends heavily on the availability and cost of cleaner fuels. According to WSC, alternative-fuel-capable vessels now account for 65% of containerships and 97% of vehicle carriers on order, measured by deadweight tonnage. That compares with just 23% across the rest of the global shipping fleet. Despite that shift, orders for conventionally fueled ships have also increased over the past year as the overall orderbook continues to expand. The mixed picture comes amid continued uncertainty over the International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which would introduce a global marine fuel standard and greenhouse gas pricing mechanism. Adoption of the framework was postponed in October 2025, with negotiations set to resume later this year. WSC argues that a global regulatory framework is needed to close the cost gap between conventional fuels and renewable and near-zero-emission alternatives while giving shipowners and fuel producers the certainty needed to invest. Without an international agreement, the industry also faces the prospect of an increasingly fragmented system of regional emissions rules, adding costs and complexity to global shipping. “Ships ordered today will be operating for decades. Shipping companies and fuel producers need certainty to make the investments that will shape the future fleet and its fuel supply,” Kramek said. The IMO is scheduled to hold its next Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting from November 30 to December 3, with a possible resumed session on the Net-Zero Framework on December 4. “We trust IMO member states can come together to deliver that framework,” Kramek said. “Every delay means increased uncertainty, making the transition harder and costlier for the global economy.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. articles.title: ID Logistics revenue jumps 25.6% in Q3 as North America drives growth
articles.summary: ID Logistics reported a 25.6% increase in revenue during the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong growth in North America and continued expansion across its international operations. The contract logistics group generated revenue of €1.18 billion, compared with €937.8 million in the same period last year....
articles.body: ID Logistics reported a 25.6% increase in revenue during the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong growth in North America and continued expansion across its international operations. The contract logistics group generated revenue of €1.18 billion, compared with €937.8 million in the same period last year. Like-for-like growth reached 25%, accelerating from 22.6% in the second quarter and 17.2% in the first quarter. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue increased by 20.9% to €3.26 billion, while like-for-like growth stood at 21.7%. The company launched 10 new operations during the third quarter, bringing the total to 27 since the beginning of the year. North America leads regional growth North America recorded the strongest regional performance, with like-for-like revenue growth of 48.1% in the third quarter. Revenue in the region reached €265.9 million. Europe excluding France generated €543.9 million in revenue, representing like-for-like growth of 23.4%. In France, revenue reached €272.3 million, up 8.3% on a like-for-like basis. Other regions reported revenue of €95.8 million, with like-for-like growth of 35.9%, partly supported by the launch of operations in Australia. Nearly 80% of ID Logistics’ business is now generated outside France. New logistics operations support expansion The company continued expanding its contract logistics network during the quarter. In the United States, ID Logistics secured a third operation for Nutrabolt, a sports nutrition and energy drinks company. The operation will be based at a dedicated 60,000-square-meter facility in Jacksonville, Florida. In Canada, the group plans to open its third site before the end of 2026. The mechanized facility, located in Eastern Canada, will handle apparel and footwear for an existing customer described as a global e-commerce leader. The Canadian site will represent ID Logistics’ first fashion logistics operation in North America. “Our business model is scaling up,” said Eric Hémar, Chairman and CEO of ID Logistics. Hémar highlighted the group’s expanding international presence, investments in technology and continued growth in new operations. Looking ahead, ID Logistics expects another year of strong growth in 2026. Its immediate priorities include increasing activity at recently opened facilities, implementing new customer projects and preparing for peak demand during Black Friday and the holiday season. The company is scheduled to publish its fourth-quarter revenue figures on January 26, 2027.

REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Thursday that seven commercial vessels were struck overnight in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, including four ships conducting oil transfers, prompting President Donald Trump to accuse Tehran of fabricating attacks to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said four vessels conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were struck simultaneously on Wednesday and caught fire. The vessels were allegedly transferring oil for an American company using routes Iran considers illegal. In a separate claim, the IRGC said three additional vessels struck naval mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires that left them disabled, according to Reuters . None of the seven incidents has been independently confirmed. Iran did not identify the ships, their owners or the American company allegedly involved. There were also no immediate details about casualties or potential oil spills. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which tracks attacks on commercial shipping in the region, has not issued new incident reports corresponding to the claims. President Trump responded Thursday by accusing Iran of inventing attacks as part of an effort to influence oil prices ahead of the November 3 elections. “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict.” The president’s accusation follows weeks of increasingly aggressive Iranian statements claiming that merchant vessels using routes outside Tehran’s control have been struck by mines or other weapons. But the absence of UKMTO reports does not necessarily mean the attacks did not occur. In its October 16 weekly assessment , UKMTO acknowledged that it was struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted were not reporting incidents directly to the organization. UKMTO said it was aware of additional attacks through other sources but could not publish warnings without sufficient verification. That reporting gap has become increasingly important as the United States and Iran offer competing accounts of what is happening in the waterway. The most significant element of Iran’s latest announcement is its claim to have targeted four vessels actively engaged in ship-to-ship oil transfers. If confirmed, the attacks would appear to mark the first reported direct targeting of an active ship-to-ship oil transfer operation during the conflict. Such transfers have become a critical part of the improvised shipping network that has allowed Persian Gulf producers to restore much of their oil exports despite repeated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Under a system operating with U.S. military assistance, tankers make short voyages through the strait, frequently with their AIS transponders switched off, before transferring cargoes to other vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman. The receiving tankers then carry the oil to international markets. The system has allowed producers to move substantial volumes of crude without relying on routes controlled by Iran, although at extraordinary cost. The International Energy Agency reported Wednesday that tanker freight costs from the Middle East Gulf to Asia had climbed above $37 per barrel, more than five times prewar levels. For a fully loaded 2-million-barrel VLCC, that translates to more than $74 million in freight costs alone. The location of Iran’s latest alleged attacks, in the northern Persian Gulf, is distinct from the Gulf of Oman transfer operations used by the U.S.-facilitated shuttle system. There is currently no independent evidence connecting the four vessels to that network. Nevertheless, a confirmed attack on vessels during cargo transfers would represent a potentially significant expansion of the threat to regional oil shipping. Iran’s latest claims also follow a series of announcements alleging that tankers have struck naval mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian authorization. Those claims have repeatedly been challenged by maritime security authorities. In its October 18 advisory , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) addressed Iranian statements that two supertankers had struck mines the previous day, saying there was “no substantiation to these claims.” U.S. Central Command has also rejected previous Iranian mine-strike announcements as false, accusing the IRGC of attempting to intimidate commercial shipping through disinformation. However, JMIC continues to warn of a credible threat of renewed mining in and around the strait’s traffic separation scheme. Its latest assessment maintains the threat level for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE, with further deliberate attacks considered highly likely. Trump’s assertion that more oil is moving through Hormuz than before the conflict also comes amid conflicting assessments of the recovery in Gulf exports. Overall Middle East oil shipments have approached or exceeded prewar levels in recent weeks, aided by an expanded network of pipelines, short-haul tanker voyages and offshore transfers. But the recovery in total exports does not necessarily mean that more oil is moving through the strait itself. According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal cited by gCaptain , flows through Hormuz, including offshore transfers, remained at approximately 82% of prewar levels, even as overall regional exports recovered. UKMTO’s latest weekly overview also recorded just 254 vessel transits during the seven days ending October 14, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. Those figures include U.S.-reported facilitated transits that UKMTO says it cannot independently verify. The figures measure different things—vessel movements, oil flows through Hormuz and overall regional exports—but illustrate the difficulty of determining how much shipping has actually recovered. Meanwhile, the security situation continues to deteriorate. UKMTO documented 12 attacks during the reporting period ending October 16, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz. One vessel was lost, two were disabled or left not under command, and the outcomes of three others remained uncertain. The escalation has included the sinking of the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride following an October 13 attack, as well as strikes on tankers operating inside the Persian Gulf. Iran’s latest announcement adds another seven potential incidents to an already incomplete picture. For now, neither Tehran’s claim that seven vessels were attacked nor Trump’s assertion that the incidents were fabricated has been independently established. What is clear is that merchant ships continue to face serious threats, even as oil producers find increasingly costly ways to keep cargoes moving. Windward intelligence report highlights tanker and tug attacks, threats to subsea cables, an emerging oil spill and a sanctioned Russian tanker testing U.S. naval restrictions. Maritime security risks across the Strait of Hormuz, Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman are expanding beyond attacks on commercial tankers, with threats now extending to subsea communications infrastructure, offshore support vessels and coastal facilities. An October 22 intelligence report from Windward Maritime identifies five developments that illustrate the widening scope of the conflict and its implications for commercial shipping, energy transportation and regional infrastructure. Iran Threatens Subsea Communications Cables Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has identified subsea internet cables crossing the Strait of Hormuz as potential targets. On October 19, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi warned that new targets and weapons would be unveiled, citing seven major communications cables beneath the strait. Windward identifies six operational cable systems crossing Hormuz, with additional systems scheduled for 2027. Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar are particularly vulnerable because their subsea communications routes to markets outside the Gulf pass through the strait. For Iraq, the vulnerability is compounded by all three operational cables landing at Al Faw. Disruptions could affect regional communications infrastructure well beyond commercial shipping. However, Windward notes that two cable systems also connect to Iran, meaning attacks could damage Iranian connectivity. Live subsea cable landings per country across the Arabian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, with countries ranked by exposure. Source: Windward Maritime AITM Platform. Small-Boat Attack Signals Changing Tactics On October 16, a Liberia-flagged Suezmax tanker was likely struck by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat approximately 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubail, Saudi Arabia. According to a UK Maritime Trade Operations advisory cited by Windward, the attack damaged the tanker's aft port quarter, although no casualties were reported. The vessel continued sailing, reportedly carrying approximately 1.09 million barrels of Saudi and UAE crude bound for Kuwait. Earlier that day, another tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile nearby, prompting the safe evacuation of its crew. Windward considers the suspected small-boat attack significant because previous incidents predominantly involved drones or projectiles concentrated around Hormuz. The development suggests threats to shipping are extending deeper into the Gulf, potentially affecting war-risk assessments for regional port calls. Tug Attack Threatens Gulf Oil Transfer Operations A Netherlands-flagged tug, identified by TradeWinds as JIF Barracuda, was reportedly struck by two unidentified projectiles northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE, on October 18. One crew member suffered minor injuries, but the tug continued its voyage. UKMTO did not attribute responsibility for the attack. Windward identifies the incident as the second tug strike since the conflict began and the 27th maritime attack recorded during October. The location is significant. Khor Fakkan, Fujairah and Sohar support extensive ship-to-ship crude oil transfers outside Hormuz. Windward estimates that these anchorages handled approximately 3.97 million barrels per day in transfers during October 12–14, representing roughly half the crude shipped from the Gulf of Oman during that period. Attacks on tugs threaten the support infrastructure needed to maintain tanker movements, cargo transfers and salvage operations. Tanker Oil Leak Threatens UAE Coastline Satellite imagery collected October 19 identified a VLCC-size tanker apparently leaking oil approximately 25 kilometers north of Umm Al Quwain. Windward observed a slick extending approximately 1.5 km behind the vessel. Its drift modeling projected possible shoreline contamination beginning October 22, with oil potentially approaching Hamriyah Port, Ajman Port, coastal mangroves and desalination infrastructure through October 24. The company cautions that its projections do not account for cleanup operations or the leak being stopped. Sanctioned Russian Tanker Tests U.S. Naval Line A Russian-flagged oil and chemical tanker approached and crossed a U.S. Navy restriction line inbound to the Gulf of Oman on October 18. According to Windward, the vessel slowed from nine knots to approximately one knot, loitered and subsequently reversed course toward the Arabian Sea on October 19. The EU- and UK-sanctioned tanker was assessed as potentially carrying approximately 65,400 barrels of naphtha. Windward describes the movement as an apparent test of the naval restriction line, although the vessel's intended destination remains unknown. Taken together, the five developments point to an increasingly complex operating environment for shipowners, charterers and marine service providers. Beyond the direct threat to vessels, the conflict is exposing vulnerabilities in the infrastructure that supports regional trade, energy exports and maritime operations.

articles.body: CSSC Offshore & Marine Engineering (Group) Company Limited (COMEC) secured RMB35.799 billion in new orders during the first nine months of 2026, exceeding its full-year contract target by a substantial margin. According to a stock exchange disclosure dated 20 October, the Chinese shipbuilder achieved 217.97% of its annual order intake target by the end of September, with contracts covering several containership classes. The company’s 2026 business plan, outlined in its 2025 annual report, had set a full-year contract acquisition target of RMB16.424 billion. The value of orders secured between January and September was therefore more than double the original target. Containership contracts included in order intake COMEC confirmed that its new orders included shipbuilding contracts for containerships with capacities of 1,900 TEU, 3,000 TEU, 5,300 TEU and 6,400 TEU. The disclosure did not specify the number of vessels contracted in each capacity class, identify the shipowners involved or provide individual contract values and delivery schedules. The RMB35.799 billion figure represents the company’s overall order intake during the nine-month reporting period and should not be interpreted as the value of containership contracts alone. The company stated that the orders were secured through its ordinary business operations and had completed the necessary internal approval procedures. Additional approval from its board of directors or shareholders was not required. Expected impact on future performance COMEC expects the execution of its newly secured contracts to have a positive impact on future cash flow and operating performance. The shipbuilder also stated that fulfilling these orders would not materially affect its operational independence or create significant dependence on the customers involved. According to the announcement, containerships are among the company’s principal products, while the counterparties to the contracts have good credit standing and the capacity to meet their contractual obligations. Nevertheless, COMEC cautioned that contract execution remains subject to uncertainties associated with changes in legislation, industry policies, pricing and market conditions. The announcement reflects contracts accumulated during the first three quarters of 2026, rather than shipbuilding agreements concluded exclusively in October.

REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo QatarEnergy has signed two long-term agreements to purchase up to 4 million tonnes of U.S. liquefied natural gas annually from Cheniere Energy through 2054, as the Gulf producer continues to grapple with damage to its own export facilities from the war with Iran. The agreements, announced Thursday, cover 2 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) each from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass facility in Louisiana and Corpus Christi facility in Texas. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054. Under the contracts, QatarEnergy will purchase the LNG on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, taking responsibility for transporting cargoes from the U.S. terminals. Pricing will be linked to the Henry Hub natural gas benchmark plus a fixed fee. The deal comes as QatarEnergy faces significant disruptions to its own LNG production following Iranian missile strikes on its Ras Laffan Industrial City in March. The attacks damaged two LNG production trains with a combined capacity of 12.8 MTPA, knocking out approximately 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy has warned that repairs could take three to five years, potentially costing $20 billion annually in lost revenue and disrupting long-term supply commitments to customers in Europe and Asia. While the U.S. contracts will not begin delivering cargoes until the early 2030s, they will give QatarEnergy an additional source of supply outside the Persian Gulf, where energy infrastructure and shipping have faced mounting threats during the conflict. QatarEnergy described the agreements as part of its broader strategy to diversify its global LNG portfolio. “This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market,” said Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Qatar’s minister of state for energy affairs and CEO of QatarEnergy. For Cheniere, the agreements secure another major long-term customer for its U.S. Gulf Coast operations. The company currently operates approximately 56 MTPA of LNG production capacity across Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi, with another 5 MTPA under construction. One million tonnes annually under the new Sabine Pass agreement remains contingent on a final investment decision for the first phase of the terminal’s planned expansion. The deal highlights QatarEnergy’s growing role not only as a major LNG producer but also as an international LNG trader, while adding another long-term source of U.S. Gulf Coast cargoes that can reach global markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. articles.body: South Carolina Ports (SC Ports) has handled the first container carrying production equipment for Isuzu North America Corporation’s new manufacturing facility in South Carolina. The shipment arrived at the Port of Charleston before moving by rail to Inland Port Greer. It marks an early logistics milestone for Isuzu’s planned production operations in Greenville County. Isuzu selected the location in 2025, partly because of its rail connection to the Port of Charleston. The company expects to begin production at the new facility in 2027. The plant will manufacture N-Series Gas, N-Series Electric and F-Series Diesel trucks. Inland Port Greer supports automotive supply chains Inland Port Greer provides rail connections between the Port of Charleston and industrial customers across the southeastern United States. The facility operates along the Interstate 85 corridor between Atlanta and Charlotte. It offers overnight rail service through Norfolk Southern six days a week, alongside 24-hour gate access. SC Ports completed a $55 million expansion of the inland port in 2025. The project added 9,000 feet of rail infrastructure and increased cargo handling capacity by 50%. Following the expansion, the terminal can accommodate up to 300,000 rail lifts annually. “Having a reliable and efficient supply chain is critical to our long-term success as we establish production operations in South Carolina,” said Yoshi Murakami, Chairman and CEO of Isuzu. SC Ports Director of Vessel Operations & Carrier Sales Tom Boyle, and Chief Commercial Officer Byron Miller recently traveled to Isuzu Global Headquarters in Yokohama, Japan. (Photo/SC Ports) Charleston strengthens automotive logistics connections The first shipment highlights the role of the Charleston–Greer rail connection in supporting automotive manufacturing investments. According to SC Ports, its facilities handle approximately 10% of containerised automotive cargo volumes in the United States, based on PIERS data. The port authority also reported that Inland Port Greer experienced 355% growth during its first decade of operations. SC Ports President and CEO Micah Mallace welcomed the Isuzu shipment and highlighted the inland port’s role in supporting industrial supply chains. The latest delivery represents the arrival of production equipment rather than the start of regular component shipments. Isuzu’s manufacturing operations are scheduled to begin in 2027.

The partners made their first move into the Korean market in 2024, deploying a Korean-flagged crew transfer vessel (CTV) for offshore wind work. The MP Corus was among the vessels brought into the market to support wind farm construction activities off the country’s southwest coast. Marco Polo Marine has also been expanding its offshore wind support fleet across Asia. In July, the company secured a multi-year framework agreement with Siemens Gamesa covering two commissioning service operation vessels (CSOVs), primarily for projects in Taiwan, with potential deployments in South Korea and Japan. articles.body: Miros Launches 3D Vessel View For Sea-State Monitoring Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 © Miros Miros, a Norwegian specialist in radar-based real-time ocean surface measurement, has introduced a 3D vessel view providing crews and operators with a consolidated view of the accurately measured sea state surrounding their vessel. The new 3D interface in WaveSystem, a wave monitoring system for weather-critical offshore vessel operations, shows where each wave measurement is taken. It brings each installed measurement source, its measurement area and the key wave values together in one intuitive display, providing a bird’s-eye view of the sea state data most relevant to safeguard operations. The feature is included for WaveSystem subscribers worldwide at no additional cost. Wave conditions can differ around a vessel due to wave direction, vessel heading, hull geometry, shielding, and measurement location. Where multiple measurement sources are installed, comparing readings can help teams clearly understand differences between measurement areas and sea conditions affecting specific working areas. Bridge and deck crew can easily assess conditions port and starboard, check the waves at a specific working area such as a gangway or ROV launch point, and spot differences between measurement areas before they affect the operation, turning a weather-critical operation into a controlled one. The visualization shows measurement sources, areas, and values in relation to the vessel. It does not represent a reconstructed 3D sea surface.

articles.body: Rhenus has introduced a smart order-picking system at its logistics hub in Strasbourg, France, to improve warehouse operations for science and technology company Merck. Developed with logistics technology specialist Signature One, the solution combines automated weight checks, light-guided picking and digital quality controls. The Strasbourg facility supports Merck’s operations in Molsheim and processes approximately 2,800 orders daily across three shifts. The new technology aims to improve order accuracy, reduce picking errors and support more efficient warehouse operations. Smart trolleys improve order preparation At the centre of the system are smart picking trolleys equipped with integrated weighing technology. Each trolley can accommodate up to 30 scales, allowing operators to check product quantities and weights during order preparation. Light-guided picking helps warehouse employees identify items more efficiently, while onboard cameras allow teams to review orders when additional checks are needed. The trolleys also feature an ergonomic design and colour-coded identification to help organise warehouse activities. “Our shared objective with Rhenus was to improve customer satisfaction by ensuring that the right quantities are picked for every order,” said Quentin Decoster, Distribution Manager at Merck’s Molsheim site. The technology is particularly relevant to Merck’s operations, where accurate order preparation and product traceability are important requirements. Further warehouse digitalisation planned The deployment marks another step in the 16-year logistics partnership between Rhenus and Merck. In 2025, the companies introduced a logistics shuttle powered by B100 renewable biodiesel between Merck’s Molsheim facility and the Rhenus hub in Strasbourg. The partners now plan to connect the smart trolleys to a wider order-preparation system. Future developments will include integration with conveyor systems, on-demand packaging equipment and other warehouse management tools. The planned improvements aim to connect warehouse processes more closely, from incoming deliveries to final customer shipments.

articles.summary: TDI-Brooks has completed a geotechnical mission, bolstering Cook Inlet LNG’s efforts to shore up Southcentral Alaska’s energy supplies.
articles.body: Vessels October 22, 2026 · 8 hours ago Cook Inlet LNG steps up Alaska energy push with TDI-Brooks survey TDI-Brooks has completed a geotechnical mission, bolstering Cook Inlet LNG’s efforts to shore up Southcentral Alaska’s energy supplies. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email N5K on back of RV Poseidon with the rig working close to it in the background Credit: Ivan Svrcek/TDI-Brooks U.S.-headquartered geotechnical and offshore survey research and service company TDI-Brooks has wrapped up a critical geotechnical campaign for Cook Inlet LNG, a strategic initiative designed to secure natural gas supplies for Southcentral Alaska, delivering vital subsurface data to support the project's anchor selection and helping bring the developer’s floating import terminal aspirations closer to reality. TDI-Brooks has concluded a geotechnical project for the Cook Inlet LNG project (CI LNG) in Cook Inlet, Alaska, providing its Neptune N5K cone penetration testing (CPT) system for an anchor site characterization study. The work supported the project developer by collecting subsurface soil data to inform anchor selection. According to the U.S. player, the study covered different locations within the project site with a scope of 16 CPTs in water depths ranging from 10 to 25 meters. Operations were conducted from the R/V Poseidon , a third-party vessel working in the region, demonstrating the firm’s ability to deploy specialized geotechnical equipment aboard locally available vessels. The Neptune N5K is part of the company’s range of portable toolkits available for deployment worldwide, which allow clients to pair regional vessel resources with TDI-Brooks’ equipment and technical expertise, providing flexible support for offshore site investigations and infrastructure projects. The Cook Inlet LNG project is an energy security initiative designed to address declining natural gas reserves in the Cook Inlet basin of Southcentral Alaska to stave off a potential energy shortfall for heating and electricity by serving as a near-term bridge solution to import gas. The project is designed to use a floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) anchored offshore east of West Foreland, near the existing Osprey production platform, utilizing existing subsea pipelines to minimize environmental and construction footprints. TDI-Brooks’ geotechnical study was done to test the seafloor soil properties to figure out how to safely anchor the FSRU and its infrastructure in Cook Inlet's harsh marine environment. The completion of this study comes months after the U.S. firm was hired by Delfin LNG to provide offshore geophysical and geotechnical survey services for the Delfin deepwater port project offshore Louisiana. articles.summary: CMA CGM’s first container train has arrived at the East-West Gate (EWG) intermodal terminal in Fényeslitke, Hungary, marking a new development in the facility’s growing role in international container logistics. The arrival follows the introduction of Maersk’s container depot and dry port services at the terminal...
articles.body: CMA CGM’s first container train has arrived at the East-West Gate (EWG) intermodal terminal in Fényeslitke, Hungary, marking a new development in the facility’s growing role in international container logistics. The arrival follows the introduction of Maersk’s container depot and dry port services at the terminal earlier in 2026. The presence of both shipping companies reflects growing interest in the terminal’s connections between European rail networks and international maritime transport. Located near the Hungarian–Ukrainian border, East-West Gate connects Ukraine’s broad-gauge railway system with Europe’s standard-gauge network. East-West Gate expands its role in container logistics The terminal was originally developed to support rail freight movements between China and Central and Eastern Europe through Ukraine. However, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 disrupted the planned transport corridor. As a result, EWG Group began exploring new markets and alternative cargo flows. The arrival of CMA CGM’s first container train represents another step in that transition. The terminal is now seeking to serve growing demand from industrial customers in eastern Hungary, particularly in the battery and electromobility sectors. These industries generate significant inbound container volumes. However, lower export volumes create challenges for repositioning empty containers. East-West Gate aims to support more balanced container flows by connecting industrial imports with other cargo opportunities in the region. New opportunities for Ukrainian agricultural exports The terminal is also exploring opportunities linked to Ukrainian agricultural exports. The war has disrupted traditional export routes, increasing interest in alternative transport options for grain and other agricultural products. EWG Group is developing solutions that could allow commodities traditionally moved in bulk to enter containerised supply chains. This approach could create additional opportunities for shipping lines, freight forwarders and agricultural exporters using the terminal. The company also aims to strengthen cooperation with international ocean carriers and other logistics partners. Through these developments, EWG Group is working to establish Fényeslitke as a connection point for maritime container logistics, intermodal transport and conventional rail freight. The announcement did not specify the volume carried by CMA CGM’s first train or confirm a schedule for future services.
