articles.title: Global Shipyard Orderbook Up 13%, China Dominates
articles.summary: "On 1 September 2026, the global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2m Compensated Gross Tonnage (CGT), up 13% from 180.0m CGT a year earlier,” says Niels Rasmussen, Chief Shipping Analyst at BIMCO.This is slightly below the all-time…
articles.body: Global Shipyard Orderbook Up 13%, China Dominates Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 "On 1 September 2026, the global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2m Compensated Gross Tonnage (CGT), up 13% from 180.0m CGT a year earlier,” says Niels Rasmussen, Chief Shipping Analyst at BIMCO. This is slightly below the all-time high of 210.4m CGT reached in May but remains above the previous record of 195.4m CGT from 2008. Much of the growth has been captured by Chinese shipyards, who secured 74% of the CGT contracted during the past year. This has further strengthened China’s position as the world’s largest shipbuilding nation. Chinese shipyards now hold 64% of the global order book while South Korean shipyards hold 19% and Japanese 6%. China’s dominance extends across the major cargo-carrying ship sectors. Its shipyards hold more than 72% of the order book in each of the six main sectors: container, tanker, gas tanker, dry bulk, other dry cargo and RoRo. Combined, these sectors account for 88% of the global order book. Their yards’ largest share is in the container ship segment, with 81% of the order book. “Container ships dominate both the order book and its growth over the past 12 months. They account for 30% of CGT on order and 68% of the increase during the past year,” says Rasmussen. Additionally, Chinese shipyards currently have better capacity coverage than their South Korean and Japanese competitors. If each shipyard’s current capacity is assumed to equal its highest annual CGT output during 2021–2025, Chinese shipyards hold orders equivalent to an average of 4.2 years of capacity. The corresponding figures for South Korean and Japanese yards are 1.9 and 1.7 years. Combined deliveries from China, South Korea and Japan peaked at 40.1m CGT in 2025, but 55.9m CGT and 60.0m CGT are currently scheduled for delivery in 2027 and 2028. Chinese yards, in particular, will have to raise output to manage the scheduled deliveries. Current capacity could therefore be assumed to equal the highest annual CGT delivered or scheduled for delivery during 2021–2030. In that case, average coverage falls to 2.1 years for Chinese shipyards and 1.6 years for both South Korean and Japanese shipyards. “China has further strengthened its position as the world’s leading shipbuilding nation, but its shipyards must raise annual output to new record highs in order to deliver. Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44.0m CGT in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m CGT delivered in 2025. The capacity expansion needed to achieve this could increase the risk of underutilisation if contracting weakens in the future,” says Rasmussen.

articles.body: Asia Gas Eastern Pacific takes wraps off first ammonia dual-fuel VLAC Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 347 1 minute read EPS / MMMCZCS EPS / MMMCZCS Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has named its first ammonia dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier (VLAC) at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, bringing the 93,000 cu m vessel closer to its commercial debut. The Singapore-based owner christened the vessel Terra Clove at the Ulsan yard, with delivery scheduled for November following sea trials. The newbuilding is the first ammonia dual-fuel commercial vessel to be registered under the Singapore flag and the first of two such ships being built by HD Hyundai for EPS. Designed to transport ammonia as cargo and burn it as propulsion fuel, the 230 m long vessel is fitted with Everllence’s 6G60ME-LGIA two-stroke engine, which completed factory acceptance testing in April and passed type approval testing in June. The ship features four cargo tanks and dedicated ammonia fuel handling and safety systems, including leak detection and emissions management equipment. The project dates back to June 2022, when EPS joined forces with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and classification society ABS to develop an ammonia-powered gas carrier. The partners have since worked on the vessel’s design, safety requirements and regulatory approval, with particular attention to ammonia handling, ventilation, emissions and crew preparedness. The milestone also coincided with EPS signing a strategic partnership with the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping during the naming ceremony. The two will collaborate on alternative fuels, dual-fuel propulsion, energy efficiency and ammonia safety, including research into methane and ammonia emissions. A joint white paper covering VLAC design, operational safety and crew training is expected later this year. The development adds to EPS’s expanding position in the ammonia carrier market. Earlier this year, the company returned to China’s Jiangnan Shipyard for two additional 90,000 cu m VLACs, scheduled for delivery in the first half of 2028. Those vessels will feature LPG dual-fuel propulsion, rather than engines designed to burn ammonia. The latest contract followed a series of six 93,000 cu m VLACs previously booked at Jiangnan, as EPS continued building up its gas carrier fleet alongside investments in alternative propulsion technologies. articles.body: Bunkering Europe Gas Tankers Maersk Tankers lines up EU backing for four VLAC ammonia conversions Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 426 1 minute read Maersk Tankers Maersk Tankers Danish shipowner Maersk Tankers has moved closer to converting four very large ammonia carriers to run on the cargo they transport after its retrofit proposal was selected for support under the European Union’s Innovation Fund. The project, known as RIPPLE, involves installing dual-fuel, two-stroke ammonia engines on four vessels in the company’s expanding gas carrier fleet. The European Commission has invited the project to begin grant agreement preparations, although the amount of funding has not yet been finalised. Crucially, Maersk Tankers said any decision to proceed would depend on securing commercial commitments from customers. The proposed conversions would allow the vessels to use ammonia as propulsion fuel rather than relying solely on conventional marine fuels. According to the Commission’s project description, RIPPLE would demonstrate the EU’s first dual-fuel ammonia retrofit on a VLAC. Speaking to Washington’s Center for a New American Security, Carino linked cable security to South China Sea tensions, but did not mention China by name. He said security of undersea cables was vital given that they carried nearly all intercontinental data flows “and that 60-67% of cyber incidents happen in our region.” “These are very important features that should be protected, so much so that we are exploring deeper cooperation with our friends in Taiwan,” Carino said, adding that the Philippines was doing so “notwithstanding our one China policy.” He said the Philippines and Taiwan were exploring “practical and more pragmatic approaches in cooperation, including knowledge-sharing and capacity building” and added: “We see this cooperation leading towards … addressing the gray-zone issues in our part of the world.” China warned the Philippines that it should “strictly adhere to the one-China Principle with real actions” and sent Taiwan a similar message, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Thursday. REUTERS/Ahmed Jadallah By Salma El Wardany Oct 22, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Saudi Arabia is in talks with foreign governments to give state-owned Aramco access to their strategic oil storage, as the kingdom seeks to make its supplies to customers more resilient during disruptions, Chief Executive Officer Amin Nasser said. The move follows a flurry of attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on key Saudi infrastructure, including drone strikes that shut down its most important pipeline for several days in September. On Wednesday , attacks on Aramco’s Shaybah oil field and Dammam airport each killed two people, according to Saudi authorities. Brent crude climbed above $112 a barrel on Thursday as the violence heightened concerns about further disruptions to Saudi supplies. “Commercial storage available through partners is limited. The larger capacity lies in what we call strategic storage owned by governments,” Nasser said in an interview with Al Arabiya on Thursday. “The Ministry of Energy is working with its counterparts in other countries to make strategic storage available for Aramco.” The company already holds commercial oil storage in South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands and Egypt’s Mediterranean export hub of Sidi Kerir. “We have maintained these overseas inventories for many years, but we are working to expand them, particularly in Asia,” Nasser said. Aramco wants to double its overseas capacity, Nasser said, without giving a timetable for the expansion or disclosing current capacity. The push forms part of a broader effort to reinforce Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure and export options during the regional crisis. Aramco currently has three main export corridors — the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, and Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean. The conflict prompted the company to begin engineering studies to increase its capacity to move crude from the Persian Gulf in the east to the Red Sea in the west to 10 million barrels a day from 7 million, alongside work on other routes, Nasser said. “We did not wait for the crisis to end,” Nasser said. articles.title: OneSubsea and oil & gas giants are unlocking deeper waters with all-electric subsea tech
articles.summary: Out with hydraulics, in with electric: OneSubsea, TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron have tested all-electric tech at depths up to 3,000 meters.
articles.body: Technology & Innovation October 22, 2026 · 12 hours ago OneSubsea and oil & gas giants are unlocking deeper waters with all-electric subsea tech Out with hydraulics, in with electric: OneSubsea, TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron have tested all-electric tech at depths up to 3,000 meters. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Brazilian waters served as testing ground for all-electric subsea technology project targeting deepwater fields down to 3,000 meters Source: OneSubsea Pushing deeper into offshore frontiers, OneSubsea, a joint venture backed by SLB, Aker Solutions and Subsea7, has cleared a critical path for deepwater development through a joint industry project with France’s TotalEnergies, Norway’s Equinor, the UK’s BP, and the U.S.-headquartered Chevron to master all-electric subsea technology designed to operate 3,000 meters below the surface. OneSubsea has completed the Brazil All-Electric Joint Industry Project (JIP) , a collaboration with TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron, supported through the National Petroleum Agency (ANP) research and development regulation, to advance fully electric subsea production technologies for applications at water depths of up to 3,000 meters. The subsea player emphasizes that electrification can create new options for designing and operating future deepwater fields by replacing hydraulic actuation with electric systems and connecting subsea equipment, well completion technology, topside controls, and digital capabilities. The Brazilian project qualified electric components and control systems for deepwater applications and demonstrated an integrated architecture extending electrification beyond the subsea tree, connecting subsea production equipment with electric well completion technology, topside controls, and digital capabilities. Representatives from the participating companies recently gathered at the OneSubsea manufacturing facility in São José dos Pinhais, Brazil, to celebrate the completion of the project through technical presentations, demonstrations of subsea and downhole all-electric technologies, and a tour of the facility where electrified subsea equipment will be assembled. Darcy Ryan , Product Manager at OneSubsea, commented: “Completing this project is an important step toward expanding the role of fully electric technology in future deepwater developments. By working closely with operators to define requirements and qualify the technology, we are creating new possibilities to simplify subsea infrastructure while providing greater control, monitoring and access to data.” As subsea developments move into deeper water and increasingly complex environments, OneSubsea points out that operators are looking for new ways to simplify infrastructure, improve control, and create greater flexibility in how future fields are designed. Since traditional hydraulic systems require extensive distribution infrastructure to operate subsea equipment, adding complexity as developments extend farther from existing facilities, the company believes that this is where all-electric can make a difference. “Conventional subsea production systems use hydraulic pressure to actuate valves and chokes, requiring hydraulic distribution infrastructure across the field. All-electric technology replaces hydraulic actuation with electric motors, eliminating the need for hydraulic fluids and reducing associated infrastructure,” elaborated OneSubsea. The firm explains that the Brazilian project demonstrates how electrification can move beyond individual components toward an integrated production architecture that connects subsea equipment, well completion technology, topside controls, and digital systems. Aside from qualifying components for applications at depths of up to 3,000 meters, the project pinpointed interfaces with newly developed and qualified SLB electric completion technologies. OneSubsea underlined: “A purpose-built master control station connects the subsea equipment with topside control and digital systems, enabling an integrated approach to monitoring and operating the production system. “This architecture can simplify field layouts and reduce overall system complexity while giving operators greater flexibility when developing longer tiebacks, more remote fields, and increasingly autonomous operations.” The company states that the completion of the project builds on more than 15 years of experience in subsea electrification and more than 5 million operating hours with electrified subsea systems. The firm’s all-electric portfolio is advancing along two complementary paths, with all-electric subsea production technology moving toward commercial deployment through Equinor’s Fram Sør project in Norway, which includes 12 all-electric subsea trees . articles.title: Global shipbuilding boom moves into overdrive
articles.summary: The global shipbuilding boom is gathering pace, with orderbooks surpassing their previous 2008 peak, Chinese yards tightening their grip on the market and tanker owners increasingly turning to inexperienced builders to secure delivery slots. New figures from BIMCO put the global orderbook at 203.2m compensated gross...
articles.body: Shipyards Global shipbuilding boom moves into overdrive Sam Chambers October 22, 2026 1 3,751 1 minute read Hengli Hengli The global shipbuilding boom is gathering pace, with orderbooks surpassing their previous 2008 peak, Chinese yards tightening their grip on the market and tanker owners increasingly turning to inexperienced builders to secure delivery slots. New figures from BIMCO put the global orderbook at 203.2m compensated gross tonnes (cgt) at the start of September, up 13% year-on-year and just below May’s all-time high of 210.4m cgt. China captured 74% of new cgt contracted over the preceding 12 months, lifting its share of the global orderbook to 64%, against South Korea’s 19% and Japan’s 6%. Containerships account for 30% of tonnage on order and 68% of the past year’s growth. BIMCO calculates that Chinese yards hold orders equivalent to 4.2 years of recent peak annual production, compared with 1.9 years in South Korea and 1.7 in Japan. Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44m cgt in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m cgt delivered in 2025 “Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44m cgt in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m cgt delivered in 2025,” said BIMCO chief shipping analyst Niels Rasmussen, warning that the necessary capacity expansion risks leaving yards underutilised when contracting eventually slows. The squeeze is already bringing new shipbuilders into the tanker market. Veson Nautical reports that 51 vessels have been ordered at newly entering yards this year, up 34% from 2025. Eleven of the 16 yards identified are Chinese. The standout is Hengli Shipbuilding, which delivered its first vessel in 2024 and now holds an extraordinary 495-ship orderbook valued at $46bn. “Owners’ willingness to place orders at yards without an established tanker track record likely reflects capacity constraints at established tanker-building yards,” observed Veson analyst Rebecca Galanopoulos. Yet, despite the rush, tanker newbuilding prices remain surprisingly affordable relative to historical peaks. Broker Affinity noted in a recent research note that VLCC newbuilding prices are still 20% to 25% below their 2008 highs in nominal terms, despite today’s unprecedented tanker earnings. Adjusted for inflation, a $160m VLCC in 2008 would cost roughly $250m today, nearly double current prices. Affinity argued that Hengli’s enormous capacity injection has restrained prices, although disappearing early delivery slots and shortages of engines and pumps could soon trigger another upward move. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group, established with registered capital of RMB2bn ($300m), has begun operations following an unveiling ceremony this week. The group will draw on businesses involved in marine propulsion, heavy engineering and shipboard equipment, including Guangzhou Diesel Engine Factory, while expanding into vessel retrofits, equipment maintenance, industrial park development, leasing and inspection services. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group has set a target of reaching about $3.9bn in business scale by 2030, according to local government-backed reporting. The launch comes alongside a major expansion of the city’s shipbuilding infrastructure. Guangzhou is developing a new marine equipment manufacturing and shipbuilding base at Longxue North in Nansha, involving investment of approximately $1.09bn. The project was launched in September and is being developed separately from the new group’s establishment. GSI is lined up to operate the facility, which is expected to be completed in 2029. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group is also lined up to participate in the development, although its financial commitment has not been disclosed. The latest move follows a series of investments by Guangzhou’s established shipbuilders to deal with bulging orderbooks. GSI recently signed an agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group to outsource hull block production, adding manufacturing capacity outside the traditional shipbuilding supply chain. The yard has also been expanding its physical footprint, with new facilities planned at Xiaohudao and Longxue North as construction slots stretch towards 2030. articles.title: A new world order emerges in LNG shipping
articles.summary: The world’s LNG trading map is undergoing its biggest upheaval in years, with the near-paralysis of Gulf exports redirecting cargoes across oceans, forcing Asian buyers towards alternative suppliers and pushing European gas prices to their highest levels since 2022. While gas prices approach $30 per million British...
articles.body: Gas A new world order emerges in LNG shipping Sam Chambers October 22, 2026 0 800 3 minutes read Teo Malnar Teo Malnar The world’s LNG trading map is undergoing its biggest upheaval in years, with the near-paralysis of Gulf exports redirecting cargoes across oceans, forcing Asian buyers towards alternative suppliers and pushing European gas prices to their highest levels since 2022. While gas prices approach $30 per million British thermal units, LNG carrier spot earnings remain remarkably weak, with the Baltic Exchange assessing the US Gulf-Europe route at just $21,200 a day last week. Nearly eight months into the Hormuz crisis, oil exporters have found ways around the chokepoint. Kpler estimates that non-Iranian Middle Eastern oil flows, including alternative routes, recovered to prewar levels last week. LNG remains a different proposition, with Qatar unable to replicate the pipelines and offshore transfers that have restored much of the region’s crude trade. Vortexa recorded just five confirmed LNG carrier transits of Hormuz last week, against a four-week average of 12. Only two were laden outbound voyages. Ras Laffan loaded five cargoes totalling 400,000 tonnes. Kpler identified 13 Qatari LNG loadings during October 1-13, but only four ships were broadcasting active AIS signals. The remaining nine were verified through satellite imagery, tug tracking and other intelligence. The Al Kharsaah, carrying Qatari LNG towards Poland via the Red Sea, came under fire from a small boat in the Gulf of Aden on October 17. Its armed security team returned warning shots, forcing the attackers to retreat. The voyage could deliver Europe’s first Qatari cargo since April. The disruption is now being measured in cancelled contracts as well as missing ships. Italy’s Edison has received force majeure notices covering 35 Qatari LNG cargoes, equivalent to 4.6bn cu m of gas, with deliveries suspended until early December. Damage inflicted on two liquefaction trains at Ras Laffan in March has also removed 12.8m tonnes of annual production capacity, with repairs potentially taking years. The US is meanwhile cementing its position as the indispensable swing supplier. American terminals dispatched 2.5m tonnes across 36 cargoes last week, according to Vortexa, while official US figures show exports surged 23% in the first half of 2026. There is an irony in the American resurgence. QatarEnergy owns 70% of Golden Pass in Texas, where an expanding export operation is helping diversify its supply portfolio beyond the troubled Gulf. Europe is capturing an increasing share of Atlantic supply. S&P Global data shows Europe and Turkey received 76 of the 143 US LNG cargoes delivered in September. Egypt has also become a major destination, taking 14 American cargoes during the month as declining domestic production increases its dependence on imported gas. The reshuffle is particularly visible in India. Oman, whose LNG terminals sit outside Hormuz, displaced the US as India’s largest supplier in September. Kpler recorded 590,000 tonnes arriving from Oman, compared with 350,000 tonnes from Nigeria and 340,000 tonnes from the US. Qatar, once India’s dominant supplier, managed just 100,000 tonnes. Not all Asian buyers are responding alike. Indian LNG imports were 7% higher year-on-year in September despite elevated prices. China, Japan and South Korea have proved more reluctant to chase expensive spot cargoes. Japan’s major utilities held 2.64m tonnes of LNG in inventory earlier this month, their highest stockpile since December 2023. South Korea is increasingly relying on coal generation, with Kpler projecting available coal plant utilisation of 63.5% in November and December. IFCHOR Galbraiths calculates that South Korean coal imports rose 14% year-on-year during January-September, while Japan’s increased 8%. China’s September LNG imports fell to 5.2m tonnes, according to Kpler, as weaker industrial demand and growing pipeline supplies reduced its need for seaborne gas. Europe has less flexibility. Gas storage was just 74.6% full this week, nearly 15 percentage points below its five-year seasonal average, with Germany at around 61%. A cold winter would intensify competition for Atlantic cargoes, particularly as the EU prepares to end remaining Russian LNG imports from January 1. Stronger European demand for US gas has shortened average Atlantic voyages, releasing vessels back into the market more quickly and depressing tonne-mile demand. Baltic Exchange assessments last week put the US Gulf-Japan route at $49,000 a day, more than twice the equivalent European route. Fleet expansion adds another complication. Flex LNG estimates the global orderbook at approximately 285 vessels, equivalent to 37% of the existing fleet, with around 95 deliveries expected next year. Beyond the immediate crisis, another geographical shift is gathering momentum. LNG Canada’s September investment decision to double capacity to 28m tonnes annually reinforces the emergence of a Pacific export corridor offering Asian customers shorter voyages than traditional Atlantic suppliers. Meanwhile, Europe’s Russian LNG ban could force Arctic cargoes towards more distant Asian destinations, creating fresh shipping demand but also logistical and sanctions-related complications. The emerging picture for LNG shipping is one of greater geographical diversification, increasingly unpredictable cargo movements and an uncomfortable mismatch between the price of gas and the value of carrying it. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Visit to OneSubsea's facilities in Malaysia Source: ANPG A multibillion-dollar oil project off the coast of Angola has passed the halfway development mark, as France’s TotalEnergies, Malaysia’s Petroliam Nasional Berhad (Petronas), Luanda-headquartered Sonangol EP, and the country’s National Agency of Petroleum, Gas and Biofuels (ANPG) headed overseas to check on the construction of critical subsea hardware for the African project. A delegation from ANPG, led by Administrator Ana Miala , together with representatives from TotalEnergies, Petronas, and Sonangol visited the OneSubsea facilities in Johor, Republic of Malaysia, at the end of last month to monitor the manufacturing of equipment that integrates the subsea production system (SPS) of the Kaminho project. The delegation included Gaspar Fernandes , Member of the Operations Committee for Block 20 of ANPG; Mutombo Dondo , Deputy Director of TotalEnergies EP Angola; Rui Rodrigues and Steven Croguennec , Directors of Block 20 at TotalEnergies EP Angola and of the project, respectively; and representatives of the Block 20/11 partners from Petronas and Sonangol. Visit to OneSubsea's facilities was made to check on the progress of the subsea production system for Kaminho; Courtesy of ANPG During the visit, the delegation confirmed the planned schedule for the arrival in Angola, starting in 2027, of the equipment currently in production at OneSubsea's facilities in Malaysia. Before its offshore installation, this equipment will be tested by Angolan OneSubsea teams at the company's testing facilities in Sonils, Luanda. Among the components being manufactured are 13 subsea Christmas trees, with a focus on safety, quality, and delivery of said equipment within the planned deadlines. articles.body: Americas Asia Europe Middle East Operations Regulatory Tankers US sanctions net widens to shipping agents and lawyers Sam Chambers October 22, 2026 0 1,297 1 minute read Washington.org Washington.org Washington has widened its crackdown on Iran’s shadow fleet, sanctioning a Greek-Panamanian law firm, shipping agents in Singapore and Dubai, and nine vessels in a move targeting the service providers behind Tehran’s commodity exports. Announcing the measures yesterday, the US Treasury said Karnakis and Karnakis had established corporate structures for shipowners moving hundreds of millions of dollars worth of Iranian oil, LPG, petrochemicals and steel. Five individuals linked to the practice have also been designated. Among the companies blacklisted is Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading, the Panama- and Greece-based manager of seven Panama-flagged bulk carriers and general cargo ships. Treasury identified Anemos, Gloris and Pride as having carried Iranian-origin cargoes over the past year. The group’s other designated ships are Destiny, Flamingo 1, Harmony and Prince. Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore was sanctioned for acting as port agent for a shipment of Iranian light crude and providing bunkering services to the shadow fleet tanker Zixuan. Treasury also linked the company to networks associated with Iranian shipping figure Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line was designated for supporting Amigoz and acting as shipping agent for a company accused of arranging Iranian petrochemical purchases. Its two UAE-flagged support vessels, Whales Diamond and Whales Pearl, were also blacklisted. The action forms part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August, which is intended to cut Iran off from international financial and shipping services. US authorities are simultaneously investigating a Greek bank’s possible links with Iran, underlining the campaign’s extension from ships and owners to lawyers, agents and financiers. The bank was not named. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Panama Canal Authority The Panama Canal reported growth in vessel traffic, tonnage and revenue in fiscal year 2026, as stronger demand from energy carriers and containerships helped lift volumes despite ongoing concerns over water availability. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits during the fiscal year ended September 30, up 4.1% from 13,404 the previous year, according to results released Wednesday by the Panama Canal Authority. Total tonnage climbed 6.5% to 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, compared with 489.2 million tons in fiscal 2025. Larger vessels continued to drive much of the growth. Ships using the canal’s Neopanamax locks accounted for 52.2% of total tonnage, with volumes through those locks increasing 8.2% year over year. The canal attributed the gains to stronger demand from energy shipping segments, solid containership performance and shifting international trade patterns. Financial results were even stronger, with total revenue reaching approximately $6.6 billion, up 16.6% from the previous year. The figures remain unaudited. The results come as the canal continues to balance growing shipping demand with water conservation measures designed to protect operations during the developing El Niño weather pattern. Despite the challenges, the canal maintained a maximum authorized draft of 50 feet throughout the fiscal year’s dry season, providing relatively stable operating conditions for shipping customers. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta said during a conference call hosted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch. The canal also announced Wednesday that it was immediately reinstating its Last-Minute Reservation service for vessels using the Panamax locks. The service allows vessels without existing reservations to secure a transit slot when one becomes available, although the canal retains discretion over whether to offer the additional capacity. The decision follows improvements in watershed conditions, with recent rainfall approaching average levels and water-saving measures helping conserve supplies. It marks another adjustment to operations following restrictions imposed earlier this year in response to below-normal rainfall. The canal recently increased daily booking capacity to 33 slots , including 10 Neopanamax slots, effective October 15. However, water availability remains a concern. The canal has warned that a continuing water deficit could require further operational adjustments, particularly if El Niño conditions intensify. During Wednesday’s call, canal executives also discussed longer-term infrastructure investments, including the proposed Río Indio Lake Project, a central component of the canal’s strategy to secure freshwater supplies for future operations. The project is part of the canal’s broader Vision 2025–2035 development plan, aimed at strengthening the waterway’s resilience and maintaining its competitiveness as global shipping patterns evolve. For now, the latest results show that the Panama Canal continues to attract growing volumes of shipping traffic, even as water management remains one of its biggest operational challenges.
